We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-2083)
response:
Mechanistic drift asks: when a learned optimizer (a small network trained via meta-learning to update another network's weights) is deployed on a task family outside its meta-training distribution, does it silently change what it is computing — not just perform worse, but shift to a qualitatively different update rule? The key concepts are (1) the inner loop, where the learned optimizer proposes weight updates during a task, (2) the outer loop, where meta-training shaped those proposals across a distribution of tasks, and (3) the gap between that meta-training distribution and inference-time tasks. Crucially, learned optimizers don't just interpolate known update rules — they implement implicit algorithms whose behavior is interpretable only in terms of the training distribution that induced them. A beginner worries about accuracy degradation; an expert worries that the optimizer may appear to be performing fine on aggregate metrics while actually executing a structurally different computation — say, switching from something resembling curvature-aware descent to a pattern-matching shortcut that happens to work on the new tasks for the wrong reasons. This is dangerous because standard generalization diagnostics (held-out loss, gradient norms) won't flag it, and because downstream models trained with a drifted optimizer inherit whatever implicit inductive bias it has silently adopted.

The core probe design is a functional dissection: hold the optimizer's weights fixed, vary the input statistics systematically (gradient magnitude, curvature spectrum, loss landscape geometry), and measure whether the optimizer's output update direction rotates in a way consistent with a fixed algorithm or jumps discontinuously — the latter is the signature of strategy switching. Concretely, you'd construct synthetic inner-loop tasks with known ground-truth optimal update rules (e.g., tasks where Adam is provably optimal vs. tasks where a momentum-free rule dominates), feed them to the learned optimizer, and check whether its updates cluster by algorithm-type in representation space, as Andrychowicz et al.'s original learned optimizer work implicitly assumed but never verified. A sharper tool is mechanistic similarity analysis borrowed from circuits-style interpretability: extract the hidden state trajectory of the optimizer network across task families and apply something like centered kernel alignment (CKA) to ask whether the internal representations at inference time on new tasks are geometrically close to those from meta-training — Nguyen et al.'s CKA work gives you a scalar similarity in [0,1] where values below ~0.4 between layers of the same architecture on different distributions reliably indicated representational restructuring. A positive result looks like this: on in-distribution tasks, CKA stays above 0.8 across all layers, update directions correlate >0.9 with the ground-truth algorithm, and the optimizer's hidden states tile a connected manifold; on out-of-distribution tasks where drift has occurred, you'd see CKA drop sharply in early layers (where input statistics are processed), update directions decorrelate, and hidden states cluster separately — a clean phase transition rather than smooth degradation. The hard part is that a negative result (no detected drift) doesn't rule out drift at a level of abstraction your probes don't reach, which is why behavioral probes must be paired with mechanistic ones.

The clearest criterion is inductive bias transplantation: if the drifted optimizer instills a different implicit prior into the inner-loop model's weight trajectory, then two models trained to identical loss by the original vs. drifted optimizer will behave differently under distribution shift, adversarial perturbation, or fine-tuning — same performance, different object. This is measurable: take the inner-loop models produced by each optimizer, freeze them, and compare their loss surfaces via sharpness metrics (e.g., the trace of the Hessian or SAM-style ε-sharpness from Foret et al. 2021); a drifted optimizer that switched from curvature-aware updates to a momentum shortcut will systematically produce sharper minima even when final training loss matches. A second criterion is fragility under mild perturbation of the new task family: if the optimizer has genuinely generalized its update rule, small parametric shifts in the task distribution should degrade performance smoothly; if it has pattern-matched to surface statistics of the new family, you'll see a cliff — this discontinuity is the failure signature, and it mirrors what Gu et al. found with in-context learning in transformers where seemingly robust behavior collapsed abruptly at distributional boundaries. A third criterion, more philosophical but operationalizable, is counterfactual dependence on the wrong features: use input ablations on the optimizer's inputs (gradient history, loss values, step count) and ask which inputs drive the update — a generalized rule should depend on curvature-relevant signals, while a drifted shortcut may depend on, say, step count or gradient sign patterns that happen to correlate with good updates on this family but carry no normative justification. Taken together, these criteria reframe the question: success requires not just low loss but that the optimizer is low-loss for the right reasons, a standard that connects directly to the broader goal of deploying learned optimizers in safety-critical pipelines where the next distribution shift may not be so forgiving.

Here is the concrete scenario: suppose the meta-training distribution consists of low-rank regression tasks, and at inference time the optimizer encounters high-rank tasks with a particular spectral structure it hasn't seen — it drifts from a rule resembling approximate natural gradient descent to one that effectively applies a fixed diagonal preconditioner tuned to the new task's gradient covariance. If the new task's data distribution happens to make that diagonal preconditioner nearly optimal (e.g., features are approximately decorrelated), the inner-loop model converges to the same loss surface geometry as it would have under the correct rule — identical weights, identical Hessian spectrum, identical generalization on the test set. No behavioral probe on the trained model detects anything, because the artifact of the computation (the weights) is genuinely the same; only the process differed. This implies that auditing pipelines which inspect only trained models — checking loss, sharpness, representation geometry, even full weight snapshots — are structurally blind to optimizer drift in the regime where the drifted strategy happens to be task-compatible, which is precisely the regime most likely to pass review and enter deployment. The implication is severe: you cannot certify an inner-loop model's provenance from the model alone, in the same way you cannot reconstruct a proof strategy from the theorem it proved — and for safety-critical systems where the next task may break the accidental compatibility, the audit has given false assurance. This calls for optimizer-level audit trails — logging the optimizer's hidden state trajectories, update direction statistics, and input-dependence patterns during training, not just the resulting weights — a requirement absent from current MLOps practice and not addressed by model cards, datasheets, or existing interpretability audits like those proposed in Raji et al. 2020.

The question of whether a sufficient statistic exists in principle runs into a hard information-theoretic wall: mechanistic identity is about which computation the optimizer implements, and two optimizers can produce identical update distributions at every step while implementing different algorithms — meaning no finite summary of input-output behavior can distinguish them, only the internal state trajectory itself carries the mechanistic witness. That said, a practically useful compression exists if you accept a weaker goal — not certifying full mechanistic identity but detecting strategy switches — and the candidate sufficient statistic is the sequence of principal subspaces of the optimizer's hidden state matrix across inner-loop steps, compressed via incremental PCA: Raghu et al.'s SVCCA work showed that ~20 principal components capture >90% of representational variance in networks of comparable size, suggesting that logging the top-20 singular vectors of hidden state at logarithmically-spaced checkpoints (steps 1, 2, 4, 8... T) would require roughly 20 × d × log(T) floats per inner-loop run, tractable for d≤512 optimizers. The compression is lossy in a specific way: it preserves the geometry of the optimizer's computational trajectory but discards the precise update magnitudes, which means it can detect the phase transitions indicative of strategy switching (sudden subspace rotation) but would miss drift that operates purely in the magnitude domain without changing direction — a known blind spot. Whether a lossless sufficient statistic exists in principle is equivalent to asking whether the optimizer's mechanistic class is identifiable from its trajectory distribution, which is generally undecidable for Turing-complete optimizers but likely decidable for the bounded-depth RNN and transformer architectures actually used (e.g., the 2-layer LSTMs in Metz et al.'s VeLO), where the hypothesis class of implementable algorithms is finite and enumerable in principle. The practical recommendation is therefore a two-tier logging scheme: store the compressed subspace sketch always, and trigger full hidden-state logging retroactively when the sketch detects a subspace rotation exceeding a threshold angle (e.g., principal angle > 30° between consecutive checkpoints), keeping storage costs near-zero in the normal case while preserving forensic capacity when drift is suspected.

Yes, and the attack surface is more accessible than it appears: because the optimizer's phase boundaries are functions of gradient covariance spectrum and loss curvature, an adversary who controls the task's data distribution or loss function can engineer those statistics directly — this is essentially a meta-level data poisoning attack where the target is not the inner-loop model's weights but the optimizer's computational mode. A concrete attack form: the adversary presents a task whose data is constructed so that the empirical gradient covariance matrix has a planted high-rank perturbation (achievable by adding adversarially chosen auxiliary examples), pushing the effective condition number of the gradient distribution past the threshold where the optimizer switches from a curvature-aware mode to a sign-gradient shortcut — the inner-loop model then trains under the wrong update rule, converging to a sharper minimum that looks fine on the provided task but is brittle to the adversary's chosen downstream perturbation. This is operationally similar to the gradient manipulation attacks studied by Manipulating the Loss Landscape (Huang et al. 2020) and meta-poisoning work by Rajabi et al., except the target is the optimizer's internal state rather than the model's weights, making it invisible to defenses that monitor weight trajectories or output distributions. The attack is particularly dangerous in federated or multi-tenant settings where a learned optimizer is shared across users — one malicious participant submits crafted tasks during the optimizer's deployment, drifting it into a degraded mode that affects all subsequent users' inner-loop training without any of them being the direct attack target. A positive detection signal would be anomalous subspace rotation in the optimizer's hidden states (detectable via the sketch logging described earlier), but an adversary with knowledge of the detection threshold could craft tasks that produce boundary-crossing drift in the update rule while keeping the hidden-state subspace rotation just below the alert threshold — a cat-and-mouse dynamic structurally identical to adversarial examples in the perception domain but operating one level of abstraction higher.

response:
Stateless inference — reinitializing the optimizer's hidden states between users — eliminates the runtime cross-user drift vector but leaves the deeper threat entirely intact: if the adversary's crafted tasks are used in continued meta-training or fine-tuning of the shared optimizer weights, the drift is baked into the weights themselves and affects all future users regardless of state reinitialization, because the phase boundaries and default computational mode are properties of the weights, not the hidden states. A correct isolation guarantee requires two distinct properties: task-level state isolation (hidden states don't persist across users, which stateless inference provides) and weight-level meta-training isolation (no single user's tasks can shift the optimizer's weights during deployment), the latter requiring that the shared optimizer be frozen at deployment and that any continued meta-training happen in a sandboxed environment with adversarial task filtering. The threat model for weight-level drift maps onto backdoor attacks in federated learning — specifically Bagdasaryan et al. 2020's work showing that a single malicious participant can implant behaviors into a shared model that survive aggregation — except here the "backdoor" is a phase boundary shift that has no trigger pattern, activates on an entire class of future tasks, and produces no anomalous output on the adversary's own tasks, making it harder to detect than classical backdoors. A formal isolation guarantee would resemble a differential privacy-style bound: the influence of any single user's tasks on the optimizer's computational phase diagram should be bounded by ε, where ε is small enough that no single participant can push the optimizer across a phase boundary — this requires gradient clipping and noise injection during any meta-update, analogous to DP-SGD but applied at the meta-level, with the added complexity that the sensitivity must be measured in algorithm-space rather than parameter-space. The uncomfortable implication is that truly safe shared learned optimizers may require the optimizer weights to be permanently frozen after meta-training, with no online adaptation — sacrificing the continual learning properties that make learned optimizers attractive in the first place, a fundamental tension between capability and isolation that has no clean resolution under current frameworks.
